name: Jumping Jacks
tierNote: Safety tier C (content.md 5.1: not in the A or B lists); census.json difficulty tier 2.

claims.text: Start standing with the feet together and the arms at the sides, with room around you to jump and swing the arms.

quotes.text: Stand with feet together and your arms at your sides. Ensure adequate space around you for safe jumping and arm movement.

claims.text: Jump the legs apart while raising the arms overhead, landing with the feet hip-width apart and the arms overhead.

quotes.text: Explosively jump while simultaneously abducting your legs and raising your arms overhead. Coordinate leg and arm movements to land with feet hip-width apart and arms overhead.

claims.text: Jump the legs back together while lowering the arms to the sides, and go straight into the next rep.

quotes.text: Return your legs to together position while lowering your arms to your sides as you land. Immediately prepare for the next repetition in continuous fashion.

claims.text: Another coach puts the feet a little wider than shoulder-width at the open position.

quotes.text: Jump both of your feet out a little wider than shoulder width apart while simultaneously bringing your arms over your head.

claims.text: Keep a slight bend in the knees, stay upright with the shoulders over the hips, and land softly.

quotes.text: Keep a slight bend in your knees and avoid locking them out.
Maintain an upright posture, your shoulders stacked over your hips, throughout the move.
Jump your feet to shoulder width or slightly wider apart and land softly with each jump.

claims.text: Common mistakes: landing with straight or barely bent knees (more joint stress), jerky landings (more impact), rushing the reps, and continuous hard jumping when tired (worse landings).

quotes.text: Landing with straight knees or minimal knee bend, which increases joint stress
Jerky or uncontrolled landings, which increases impact stress and injury risk
Moving too quickly and sacrificing form for speed or total repetitions
Performing continuous high-intensity jumping when fatigued, which compromises landing mechanics

claims.text: The quads and glutes drive the jump; hamstrings, calves, shoulder and core stabilisers assist.

quotes.text: Quadriceps – primary driver of knee extension and jumping power
Glutes – generate hip extension power for vertical propulsion
Hamstrings Calf Muscles Shoulder Stabilizers Core Stabilizers

claims.text: Easier: step out instead of jumping, or use smaller arm movements.

quotes.text: Beginners can perform step-out jacks (stepping instead of jumping) or reduced arm movements to lower impact while still developing cardiovascular fitness.

claims.text: Work in intervals of 30 to 60 seconds with short rests.

quotes.text: Perform jumping jacks in intervals: 30-60 seconds of work followed by brief rest periods.

claims.text: Harder: jump higher or faster; easier: drop the arm swing or step side to side.

quotes.text: Increase the difficulty by jumping higher or faster, by incorporating resistance bands, or by combining the move with squats, squat thrusts, and planks. Or pull back as needed by taking out the arm swing or replacing the jump with a side-to-side step.

claims.text: Use a flat, even surface; rubber or grass absorbs shock better than concrete or asphalt.

quotes.text: Always choose a flat and even surface for all jumping jack variations. Surfaces like rubber or grass absorb shock more effectively than cement or asphalt.

claims.text: Keep the posture; don't slouch or twist the toes outward.

quotes.text: Remember to maintain your posture and avoid slouching or twisting your toes outward.

claims.text: Jumping jacks also work the shoulder muscles, front and back deltoids included, as the arms are raised overhead. That the side deltoids lift the arms is an inference from the movement.

quotes.text: Shoulders. Jumping jacks also work your shoulder muscles in different areas, including anterior and posterior deltoids.
Explosively jump while simultaneously abducting your legs and raising your arms overhead.

sources.title: Break It Down: The Jumping Jack (Experience Life, Life Time)
How to Do Jumping Jacks (WebMD; medically reviewed by a DPT)

plate.viewWhy: The census plate is two poses that differ only in the frontal plane: feet together and arms down (c1) vs feet apart and arms overhead (c2).
plate.frames: Two-pose plate (census note): closed (feet together, arms at the sides) and open (feet apart, arms overhead); the airborne moment is not drawn.
plate.start: Standing tall, feet together, arms at the sides (c1); shoulders over hips (c5).
plate.end: Landed with the feet apart, hip-width (c2) to a little wider than shoulder-width (c4); arms overhead (c2); knees slightly bent (c5); toes forward (c12).

checkpoints.label: Soft knees
checkpoints.what: Land with a slight bend in the knees, never locked.

checkpoints.label: Arms overhead
checkpoints.what: Arms rise overhead as the feet jump apart.

mistake.why: WebMD names it with slouching (c12). NASM's first mistake, landing with straight knees (c6), needs a side view, which this front plate lacks.

topFault.what: Landing with straight or barely bent knees.

tells.text: Shoulders stay stacked over your hips

tempo.text: Continuous reps (c3) in 30 to 60 second intervals (c9); no source gives a cadence.

setup.step: Stand with your feet together and your arms at your sides.
Jump your feet apart as your arms go overhead.
Jump back together as your arms come down, and go again.

handlingMistakes.fix: Keep a slight bend and land softly.
Slow down and keep your form.

rows.means: They push you up off the floor.

risks.risk: Stiff-kneed or jerky landings add stress to the joints.
Hard surfaces like concrete absorb less shock than rubber or grass.

libraryDiff.why: Library: quads primary; side_delts secondary. NASM lists quads and glutes as primary (c7); glutes are proposed as a secondary. For the shoulders, WebMD names the front and back deltoids and NASM 'shoulder stabilizers' (c7, c13); no source names the side delts, but the arms rise out to the sides overhead, which is the side delts' action. side_delts is kept as a MECH/WEAK reading (c13). A proposal for the LIB data card.

anchorNote: NASM Exercise Library jumping jacks page read in full; Experience Life (Life Time) and WebMD (DPT-reviewed) read in full. No PubMed technique study found.

loadProgression.text: Work in 30 to 60 second bursts; jump higher or faster to progress.

unsourced: Where the foot lands (ball vs whole foot).
notes: Open-position width: NASM says hip-width (c2), Experience Life a little wider than shoulder-width (c4). The plate draws about shoulder-width, between the two; the text says 'apart' and does not give a width.
The 'Shoulders' zoom label row uses c13 (WEAK) because the deltoid naming is general.
